meta.ogDescription: Credited everywhere to Walt Disney and true to his ethos, but no dated speech, interview, or letter pins the exact wording. Earliest citation: a 1982 compilation.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1901–1966 · American animator, film producer & co-founder of The Walt Disney Company
answer.sourceLine: Widely and credibly credited to Disney and squarely in keeping with his ethos, but no primary source — a dated speech, interview, or signed letter — has been pinned to this exact wording. The earliest citation that can be checked is a secondary compilation, Derek Walker’s Animated Architecture (1982), published 16 years after Disney’s death.

source.heading: The sourcing behind the Disney line
source.excerpt: It’s kind of fun to do the impossible.
trail: Wikiquote lists the line in its Sourced section, but the citation it gives is a secondary compilation — Derek Walker’s Animated Architecture (1982), p. 10 — not a Disney primary source.
Disney’s official fan organisation, D23, reproduces the quote with the bare tag “—Walt Disney” and no speech, date, or publication behind it.
A search of Quote Investigator returns no entry adjudicating this line — it has not been traced to a first documented use.
Every verifiable citation post-dates Disney’s December 1966 death, so the exact wording cannot presently be tied to anything he is documented to have said in his lifetime.
source.excerptNote: The line circulates as a standalone aphorism; no surviving Disney speech, film, or letter is documented to place it in a fuller sentence or context.
source.rightsNote: The wording is credibly Disney’s but cannot be tied to a specific dated, published work: the earliest checkable citation is a 1982 secondary book. Because the first-publication of the exact wording is unestablished, no copyright status is asserted here — if it derives from a genuine 1960s Disney statement it would be post-1930 and in-copyright to the Disney estate, not public domain.

author.bio: Walt Disney (1901–1966) was an American animator, film producer and entrepreneur who pioneered the modern animated feature and built the Disney studio and theme-park empire. A relentless innovator behind Steamboat Willie, Snow White and Disneyland, he became a byword for turning far-fetched ideas into reality — which is exactly why optimistic “do-the-impossible” lines gravitate to his name.

misattribution.heading: The sourcing problem
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Disney is plausible and near-universal — the issue is not who, but the absence of a verifiable where. The line is routinely presented as a firmly-documented Disney statement when the paper trail is thin.

items.why: Quote sites and posters imply a settled provenance, but the earliest citation anyone can check is Derek Walker’s Animated Architecture (1982) — a secondary book published 16 years after Disney died, not a Disney speech, film, or letter.

items.who: Dealer listings citing a ‘1966 signed letter’
items.why: Some autograph dealers advertise a Disney letter bearing the line, but such claims rest on the seller’s own provenance and are not independently corroborated primary sources — treat them with caution rather than as documentation.

misattribution.truthLine: Best read as credibly attributed but not primary-sourced: everywhere in Disney’s name and true to his spirit, yet not pinned to anything he is documented to have said, per Wikiquote.

context.heading: Why it stuck to Disney
lead: Whatever its exact origin, the sentiment fits Disney better than almost anyone: a career built on being told animation, sync sound, feature-length cartoons and a walk-through theme park couldn’t be done — and doing them anyway. That resonance is precisely why the line adheres to his name so effortlessly, and why it needs no source to feel true.

The same resonance is what makes it a textbook ‘magnet’ quote: an upbeat, frictionless aphorism that gets pinned to a famous optimist and then propagated by quote databases faster than anyone stops to ask for a citation.
context.pull: Everywhere in his name, true to his spirit — and sourced to no documented thing he said.
